generation.hypothesis: Liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu will selectively replace Ti/V-rich channels with Cu while preserving refractory ligaments and forming a W-rich interfacial barrier. The resulting aligned, bicontinuous RHEA–Cu composite should suppress interfacial voiding, conduct heat better than the untreated precursor, exceed pure W above about 650 °C, and provide RHEA ligaments with greater He-blister resistance than W.
generation.material_initial_state: The precursor will be nominally equiatomic, single-BCC WTaVTi with directionally solidified W/Ta-rich dendrites occupying about 70 vol.% and connected Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels occupying about 30 vol.%.
generation.intervention: The precursor will undergo liquid-metal dealloying by immersion in molten Cu, using the Ti-rich interdendritic regions as preferential sacrificial pathways for Cu ingress and directional channel formation.
generation.conditions: Dealloying will be conducted near 1200 °C in a sealed vacuum environment. Thermal performance will be considered from room temperature to about 800 °C, with behavior above 1000 °C treated only as extrapolative. Irradiation screening will use 25 keV He+ implantation to fluences near 8 × 10^17 atoms cm−2.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention should produce an aligned bicontinuous architecture containing roughly 64 vol.% BCC WTaVTi-based RHEA ligaments and 36 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels. An approximately 300 nm W-rich interlayer should form at RHEA/Cu interfaces, with minor Ti-rich HCP precipitates behind it.
generation.mechanism: Ti should preferentially mix with Cu and dissolve from interdendritic regions, whereas comparatively Cu-immiscible W, Ta, and V should remain in continuous ligaments. Continued Ti extraction should trap W at the reaction front, creating a passivating interlayer that arrests exchange and stabilizes bonding. Aligned Cu channels should provide efficient heat paths, while reduced diffuse interfacial mismatch and increasing lattice transport should raise conductivity with temperature. Lattice distortion, compositional complexity, and high ligament strength should alter defect migration and recombination, reducing He-driven swelling and cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thermal conductivity should rise from an untreated value near 20 W m−1 K−1 to about 75 W m−1 K−1 at room temperature, approximately 120 W m−1 K−1 near 650 °C, and 140 W m−1 K−1 near 800 °C. RHEA ligaments should show roughly 30% less swelling at blistering than W and delay blistering from about 8.0 to 8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2.
generation.baseline: Comparators will include untreated WTaVTi, pure W, pure Cu, conventional W–Cu composites, and WTa and WTaV for irradiation comparisons.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis will apply to directionally segregated WTaVTi processed near 1200 °C. Irradiation claims will be limited to low-energy He+ screening of precursor dendrites as ligament proxies, not the finished composite, neutron exposure, or vacancy-driven void swelling. Composite strength will remain unclaimed.
generation.uncertainty: The W-rich layer may not remain uniformly passivating over millimeter-scale penetration, potentially causing incomplete replacement or residual interfacial defects.

falsification_experiment.design: Process matched precursor sections with and without molten-Cu dealloying, then compare architecture, conductivity, and He response against pure W and conventional W–Cu controls.
measurements: SEM/TEM-EDS and XRD for Cu replacement, phase continuity, and the W-rich interface
AFM swelling and blister/crack onset after 25 keV He+ implantation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be rejected if continuous Cu channels and a W-rich interface do not form, or if conductivity fails to exceed untreated WTaVTi substantially and pure W near 650–800 °C, or if RHEA dendrites do not reduce swelling or delay blistering relative to W.
